analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to share downloadable blueprints for 3D-printing a gun online.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make it a federal crime to share downloadable gun blueprints online, has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since June 2025 with no action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds a new federal crime: anyone who intentionally distributes, over the internet, digital files (such as CAD files) that can automatically program a 3D printer to make a firearm or finish one from an unfinished frame or receiver would be breaking the law. It is aimed at the spread of undetectable, untraceable homemade guns — guns that carry no serial numbers, can be largely plastic, and can be made by people who failed or never took a background check. The bill was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has remained ever since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who ride public transit, send children to school, or live in communities affected by gun violence benefit from fewer untraceable, undetectable plastic guns. Law enforcement also benefits: guns with serial numbers can be traced to solve crimes, while 3D-printed guns cannot. People legally barred from buying guns — felons, domestic abusers — are the ones who lose a workaround.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime to distribute, online, digital files that can automatically program a 3D printer to produce a firearm or complete one from an unfinished frame or receiver.
It addresses the fact that 3D-printed guns have no serial numbers, so they cannot be traced by law enforcement when used in crimes.
It responds to the risk that plastic 3D-printed guns could evade metal detectors at airports and other security checkpoints.
It targets access by people legally barred from owning guns — such as felons and domestic abusers — since 3D printing bypasses the background-check system entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who wants to share or download printable gun blueprints online, and makers of 3D printer plans who would face federal criminal liability for distributing gun files. Gun-rights advocates argue the restriction also touches free-speech interests in publishing computer code.

drawbacks.text: Restricting the online distribution of digital files raises free-speech concerns, since the same CAD files are expressive computer code; the bill's findings argue the restriction targets untraceable firearms rather than protected speech, but courts weigh such speech claims seriously.
The ban covers internet and World Wide Web distribution only, so files could still be shared offline or through other channels, limiting how much it reduces access to printable gun plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is preventing untraceable, possibly undetectable guns from spreading while background checks and traceability still work; the main cost is real tension with free-speech concerns about restricting publication of digital files, and the practical reality that determined users could share files by other means or abroad. A one-sentence ban is simple but narrow, and it does nothing about files already in circulation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced the bill on June 25, 2025 and, the same day, read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.
No further action appears in the record: the bill has not received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
All 23 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents, so the bill lacked the Republican support needed to move in a Senate that typically requires 60 votes to advance most legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has gained a final result; the practical effect of the stall is that online distribution of printable gun blueprints remains unrestricted, which serves those who host or share those files and anyone who obtains guns through them.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 22 Senate Democrats plus one independent to cosponsor it.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 25, 2025 and has taken no action on it since; its chair controls whether the bill gets a hearing or a vote.

for.name: Senate Majority Leader John Thune
for.what_they_did: Controls which bills reach the Senate floor; has not brought the bill up for consideration (widely reported, standard floor-control role).

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents — 22 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican senators signed on, leaving the bill with no identified support on the Republican side of the Senate [S3].

industries.note: The bill criminalizes distributing firearm CAD files online, restricting what members of these communities can share. Ordinary printer users and makers who never touch firearms are not directly restricted, but the speech interest is theirs.

industries.industry: Unlicensed ghost-gun sellers and file distributors
industries.note: Anyone distributing printable-gun blueprints online would face federal criminal liability. This is the bill's intended target.
The bill does not restrict licensed sales, and its findings say untraceable guns interfere with lawful commerce in firearms, so established licensed dealers have little at stake either way.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action five months after introduction, and a Senate that generally requires 60 votes to advance most bills, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; the most likely path is that it dies in committee at the end of the 119th Congress, as similar versions have in past sessions.
